cards.title: Before we design new provinces
cards.author: Ashtar Ausaf Ali
cards.why: Essential for Pakistan Affairs and Governance questions concerning federalism, provincial autonomy, and the constitutional amendment process.
cards.summary: The government proposal to decide on creating new provinces via a national referendum overlooks essential constitutional procedures. Under the Constitution, altering provincial boundaries requires a two-thirds majority in Parliament as well as in the affected provincial assembly. A national popular vote cannot replace this provincial veto designed to protect residents from unwanted administrative changes.
key_facts: Articles 238 and 239 require a two-thirds majority of the total membership of each house of Parliament for a constitutional amendment.
Article 239(4) mandates that any bill altering provincial limits must secure a two-thirds majority in that provincial assembly before presidential assent.
Article 48(6) allows a national referendum on matters of national importance, but it cannot override the provincial assembly veto.
text: THE interior minister’s call for a referendum on creating new provinces, followed by the information minister’s press conference, seemingly puts the cart before the horse.

Consider a citizen told that a new province will bring government closer to their home. What does that mean to them? Will their land dispute be heard more expeditiously or decided more justly? Who will collect their taxes, and how will those revenues be spent? What does this vision of new provinces look and feel like? What will the new administrative arrangements cost, and who will pay? So far, the answers to these questions seem to vary depending on each province.

Without defining what new provinces would actually mean for everyday citizens, a binary question posed nationally can’t provide meaningful insight into the change Pakistanis want. When developers market a new housing scheme, they show prospective buyers what they intend to build. Here, it seems, citizens may be asked to buy into something before knowing what they are buying.
Citizens may be asked to buy into something before knowing what they are buying.

The Constitution already prescribes how provincial boundaries may be altered. Under Articles 238 and 239, a constitutional amendment requires a two-thirds majority of the total membership of each House of Parliament. Article 239(4) further requires any bill altering a province’s limits to secure a two-thirds majority of that provincial assembly’s total membership before presidential assent.

A national majority through referendum may favour a change whose costs fall chiefly on the people of one particular province. This safeguard gives the people most directly affected, through their elected representatives, a decisive voice. It is, in effect, a constitutional veto.

Article 48(6) permits a referendum on a matter of national importance, following approval by a joint sitting of parliament, while Article 48(7) provides for legislation governing its procedure. Yet neither parliamentary approval for a referendum nor its result can substitute for the legislative majorities mandated by Article 239. The question remains: can a referendum, by itself, effect the extensive constitutional changes that creating new provinces would entail?

The case for a new province should begin with the grievances arising from existing arrangements. If citizens travel hours to reach hospitals or government offices, publish the travel times and service gaps. If districts complain of unequal investment, disclose what was allocated and spent. If communities seek greater control over decisions affecting them, identify the powers they require.

Article 140A already obliges provinces to devolve political, administrative and financial responsibility and authority to elected local governments. Proponents must therefore demonstrate what a new province could achieve that meaningful devolution and stronger district administration cannot.

Every proposal should be accompanied by an administrative map and five- and 10-year financial projections. Which districts and divisions would be regrouped? Where would headquarters be located? How many officials would be required, and what would their offices cost? Who would collect provincial revenues, and within which jurisdictions? How would water resources and gas allocations be determined? Do we have answers ready for these vital questions?

The judicial implications deserve equal attention. What high court facilities, district courts and subordinate courts would need to be established or reorganised? What would buildings, judges, staff and operations cost? Where would litigants go, and what would become of pending cases? Surely, access to justice must be among the measures by which any promise of bringing government closer to citizens is judged.

Financial projections must establish what each administration could realistically raise, the federal transfers it would require, and the consequences for National and Provincial Finance Commission arrangements. Water entitlements, mineral and energy revenues, public assets, debts and pension liabilities cannot be left unresolved. Nor can the implications for employment, investment and public services, or the question of who bears the cost of transition, and keeps services running.

An independent commission could examine these matters, publish its evidence and assumptions, and conduct hearings across affected districts. A referendum confined to a proposed province would exclude others whose finances and institutions may be altered. Conversely, a province-wide tally could obscure substantial differences between districts. Hearings and forums would allow communities on both sides of any proposed boundary, including minorities and those distant from seats of government, to share what they want and why.

If the evidence supports creating a new province, a clearly defined proposal should then be placed before the legislatures whose consent the Constitution requires. Elected representatives must vote publicly and remain answerable to their constituents for the boundaries, costs and commitments they approve.
At this critical juncture in our nation’s history, we ought to think before we leap.
The writer is a former attorney general of Pakistan.
Published in Dawn, November 21st, 2026

cards.title: Muslim populations
cards.author: Rafia Zakaria
cards.why: Offers critical demographic and migration statistics for essays and Current Affairs questions on population management and youth employment.
cards.summary: Demographic projections indicate that Muslims will become the largest global religious group by 2035 and reach 3.6 billion by 2070. Pakistan is projected to overtake Indonesia to become the world's most populous Muslim-majority state. However, this high growth fuels a youth bulge that struggles with severe domestic job shortages and rising migration.
key_facts: The Pew Research Centre report projects Muslims will overtake Christians globally by 2035 and reach 3.6 billion by 2070.
Pakistan is projected to surpass Indonesia as the nation with the largest Muslim population.
The global fertility rate is 3.1 for Muslim women compared to 2.5 for Christian women.
Official figures show more than 762,000 individuals left Pakistan last year to seek employment abroad.
text: BY 2035, Muslims will overtake Christians to become the largest religious group in the world, according to the Pew Research Centre’s report The Future of World Religions: Population Growth Projections, 2020-2070. The report also projects that, at the current rate of population growth, by 2070, there will be 3.6 billion Muslims and slightly less than 3bn Christians globally. And Pakistan will have the largest Muslim population.
Presently, the average fertility rate for Muslim women is 3.1 and 2.5 for Christians. At 24, Muslims also have a younger median age than Christians, whose median age is 31.

On the face of it, many would consider overtaking Christianity to become the largest religious group cause for celebration. But what might temper the sentiment is that power and sway in world affairs largely elude the Muslim world. The Muslim population in both South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa is growing. Likewise, the fertility rate for Christians in sub-Saharan Africa is much greater than it is in Europe.

Moreover, the Democratic Republic of Congo is expected to surpass the US as the country with the largest Christian population. At the same time, Pakistan will overtake Indonesia as the largest Muslim country. Both Pakistan and DRC are struggling nations, and the lives of their inhabitants will not be made any better as populations grow.

In Pakistan, high population growth is causing what demographers call the ‘ youth bulge ’, with millions of young people without jobs. Official data in Pakistan shows that last year alone more than 762,000 — mostly young — people left the country to work abroad. This situation is likely to become complicated in the coming years.
While the majority of migrants find work in Arab countries — that have their own labour restrictions — those going to Europe and the US must increasingly contend with social and cultural barriers.

Islamophobia is on the rise in large parts of Europe and the US, where Muslims are treated with suspicion. In a sense, the Pew study raises more questions than it answers. Islam may become the dominant faith, but will Muslims be equal to non-Muslims in terms of human dignity?
Power & sway in world affairs largely elude the Muslim world.
The situation in richer or more educated Muslim countries is quite different. For instance, fertility rates in Iran, Turkiye, Indonesia, Tunisia, and the UAE have dropped to below replacement levels.

But this will pose different problems — similar to those in the West, where ageing populations challenge the state through diminishing human labour and high healthcare and other costs for older people. So, while some countries like Pakistan must figure out what to do with their surplus of young people, others will have to figure out how to handle ageing generations.

Each situation also carries political risks. In Turkiye, falling fertility rates threaten the ethnic balance — with parts of the country having higher fertility rates than others. This is likely to create problems for a country where the Turkish identity tends to subsume other groups numerically, politically, and culturally.

Meanwhile, recent revolts led by the Gen Z cohort in South Asia reveal the peril that restless and frustrated young people pose to regional states. No matter what tactics repressive regimes in South Asia employ to quell the protests, the dissatisfaction felt by young people is real and cannot be ignored.

Pakistan may not have seen the kind of momentous Gen Z movements that led to the collapse of governments in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and Nepal. But its youth bul­ge continues to grow, and in the coming years, un­­less the state ta­­k­es steps to satisfy the demands of young people, the threat of revolutionary moveme­nts will only increase — a situation that radical Islamist groups can exploit by tapping into the religious sentiments of angry youth. Keeping that threat in mind, South Asia must work not only to create more employment opportunities for its young but also to promote the tolerance associated with Sufi traditions.

A change in numbers does not always predict a change in global power dynamics. But in this case, the figures do provide justifiable grounds for pointing out the inequity that exists between Muslims and the adherents of other dominant faiths.

Pakistan will soon be the country with the most Muslims. The pitfalls are obvious as resources shrink for a growing population. The silver lining is that, if the state ensures better opportunities for its youth, it will have a greater chance of producing future leaders in world affairs.
The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.

cards.title: A judiciary for the voiceless
cards.author: Altamush Saeed, Eiraj Hassan
cards.why: Valuable case study material for judicial activism, animal welfare jurisprudence, and environmental governance in Pakistan.
cards.summary: Pakistani courts have established progressive jurisprudence recognizing animal sentience and the need for humane treatment. High court rulings have ordered the protection of captive wildlife and directed municipal authorities to halt poisoning stray dogs. Instead of culling, courts have pushed for scientific sterilisation and vaccination programs to control rabies.
key_facts: The Islamabad High Court recognized animal sentience in the 2020 Kaavan judgement (Islamabad Wildlife Management Board vs Metropolitan Corporation Islamabad).
Justice Khadim Hussain Soomro recognized animal sentience in Nelofar vs Chief Commissioner ICT.
Punjab adopted the Animal Birth Control Policy following judicial proceedings before Justice Ayesha Malik and Justice Shahid Karim.
The WHO, FAO, and World Organisation for Animal Health have set 2030 as the deadline to end human deaths from dog-mediated rabies through mass dog vaccination.

vocab.meaning: the ability to feel, perceive, or experience subjectively
an animal used for pulling loads
killing selected animals to reduce group numbers

text: FROM Islamabad to Lahore, from Rawalpindi and Multan to Karachi, Pakistan’s courts have been writing the same story. It began with the Kaavan judgement in Islamabad. In Lahore, Punjab’s Animal Birth Control Policy took shape before the division bench of Justice Ayesha Malik and was enforced by Justice Shahid Karim in Eiraj Hassan vs Government of Punjab. Back in the capital, Justice Khadim Hussain Soomro recognised animal sentience in Nelofar vs Chief Commissioner ICT. Justice Malik Javed Iqbal Wains has since taken up the cause of donkeys and other draught animals, Justice Shahid Karim has protected endangered monkeys, and the honeybee is now before the courts. Judges in different cities, years apart, have reached the same conclusion. The law must protect those who cannot protect themselves.

Kaavan spent more than three decades at Islamabad’s Marghazar Zoo, much of it in chains and, after his companion Saheli died in 2012, alone. In 2020, in Islamabad Wildlife Management Board vs Metropolitan Corporation Islamabad, the Islamabad High Court under chief justice Athar Minallah ordered his release along with the other animals at the zoo, and held that animals are sentient beings whose interests the law must respect. Every case since has built on that ruling.

In Punjab, the fight was over stray dogs, which municipal bodies had long met with poison and bullets. The killing never ended rabies. The WHO, the FAO and the World Organisation for Animal Health have set 2030 as the target for ending human deaths from dog-mediated rabies, and they rely on mass vaccination of dogs to get there. Litigation before the division bench of Justice Ayesha Malik helped produce a policy of sterilisation and vaccination. Culling continued anyway, until Justice Shahid Karim ordered the government in Eiraj Hassan to implement the policy in letter and spirit.
Taken together, these cases show that animal rights sit comfortably alongside human and environmental rights.

In Nelofar, decided on April 28, the IHC was shown photographs of dead dogs piled in a vehicle attributed to the Capital Development Authority. Justice Khadim Hussain Soomro banned the poisoning, shooting and indiscriminate killing of stray dogs in the capital and ordered the ICT policy enforced. The authorities were told to carry out an area-wise survey of the dog population, keep records of every animal captured, sterilised, vaccinated or euthanised, and frame procedures for capture and sheltering. He held that an animal is a sentient being entitled to be spared unnecessary pain and suffering, and that euthanasia must remain a rare exception.

Justice Soomro also reminded the state that mercy towards animals is rooted in the Quran and Sunnah. The Quran says every creature on earth and every bird that flies on its wings forms a community like our own (6:38). Surah An-Nahl, named after the bee, describes how God inspired the bee to build its home and bring forth a drink that heals (16:68-69). The Prophet (PBUH) reportedly spoke of a woman punished for starving a cat and a man forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog. Article 227 of the Constitution requires our laws to conform to these injunctions, so a court that protects animals is applying the Constitution as written.

The same reasoning now reaches working animals. The Pakistan Economic Survey counts close to six million donkeys, alongside mules and horses. They haul bricks from kilns and pull carts through traffic in summers that cross 45°C, often without water, shade or veterinary care. In Altamush Saeed vs Government of Punjab, Justice Malik Javed Iqbal Wains has begun to set out their rights. For the families who depend on them, a healthy animal is also a secure income.

The courts have looked beyond our borders too. CITES-listed rainforest monkeys from Brazil were brought into Pakistan illegally, and half of the original 26 have died here. When the government tried to move the survivors from a rescue centre in Karachi to the Lahore Zoo, Justice Shahid Karim stayed the transfer in June 2025. Justice Khalid Ishaq later made the order final. WWF Pakistan has since recommended a species-appropriate sanctuary for the survivors and a study of whether they can be returned to Brazil.

The newest case is about the bee. The FAO estimates that three in four of the world’s food crops depend at least partly on pollinators, and heavy pesticide use is wiping out colonies here. Losing them would hit our food supply directly, and it would ruin the beekeeping families, many of them in Multan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, whose income depends on healthy colonies. Protecting the bee means protecting the farmer and the food on our tables.

Taken together, these cases show that animal rights sit comfortably alongside human and environmental rights. The One Health approach, backed by the WHO, FAO, UNEP and the World Organisation for Animal Health, treats the health of people, animals and ecosystems as one. Its reasoning is simple: most new infectious diseases in humans come from animals, so the way we keep, trade and treat them is a public health question. A vaccinated dog protects a child from rabies. A healthy donkey keeps a family fed. Articles 9, 9A and 14 guarantee life, a healthy environment and dignity, and the courts have recognised that these guarantees mean little while animals around us suffer.

Public pressure mattered too. The singer Cher campaigned for Kaavan for years and co-founded Free the Wild to press his case. In November 2020 she came to Islamabad to see him off to a sanctuary in Cambodia, where he now lives among other elephants. She brought the world’s attention to him, and a Pakistani court set him free.

The judiciary has done its share, but orders on paper still meet resistance on the ground. In September, a contempt petition had to be filed in Nelofar and in the Eiraj Hassan case because the killing of dogs in Islamabad and Lahore had not stopped. Governments now need to fund the policies the courts have upheld, train the staff who carry them out, and act against officials who ignore court orders. Parliament should replace the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act of 1890. The rest falls to us, in how we treat the animals we live alongside. The Quran calls them communities like our own, and our courts have begun to treat them that way.
The writers were counsel and petitioner in several of the cases discussed.
Altamush Saeed is a lawyer who holds an LLM in animal law, environmental law and human rights law and teaches animal law and food law at Kinnaird College, Lahore.
Eiraj Hassan is a social media manager for the PSL at the Pakistan Cricket Board.
Published in Dawn, November 21st, 2026

cards.title: Chinaman or doosra
cards.author: Shahzad Sharjeel
cards.why: Provides contextual viewpoints for essays on comparative political systems, governance models, and Pakistan-China ties.
cards.summary: Pakistani decision-makers often look admiringly at China's centralised political model to deliver rapid economic progress. This top-down authority appeals to leaders who want to take difficult actions without facing multiparty resistance. However, trying to copy such centralized control ignores the realities of Pakistan's distinct constitutional and societal makeup.
key_facts: China and India are two large neighbouring economies that started modern development around the same time as Pakistan and expanded significantly faster.
China operates a centralised political system, whereas India and Pakistan follow multiparty systems.
China expanded its global economic reach through mass export manufacturing of affordable consumer goods.
